In the scenario, a vehicle already has dents and mismatched paint on one side. The owner later reports a low-speed incident and describes every visible defect as part of the new event. The claim includes an unusually broad repair estimate and documents whose dates do not line up with the reported loss.

The first review concerns consistency. The adjuster compares the reported direction and force of impact with the height, location, and shape of the damage. Fresh collision damage may show a coherent transfer pattern, broken fasteners, exposed material, or debris, while older damage can show oxidation, dirt accumulation, previous filler, or unrelated wear. These are clues, not automatic conclusions, and they should be documented without accusing the claimant prematurely. Photographs taken before the loss, prior inspection images, service records, and earlier estimates can establish what was present before the incident.

The second review concerns the supporting paperwork. A questionable file may contain an invoice from a shop that did not inspect the vehicle on the stated date, duplicate photos, a receipt with inconsistent formatting, or an estimate that includes parts unrelated to the impact. A legitimate process verifies the shop, preserves the originals, obtains an independent inspection when needed, and asks the claimant to explain discrepancies. Staff should never suggest a preferred story or tell a customer which facts to omit.

The third review concerns the event itself. Investigators may compare the account with police records, witness statements, telematics, nearby camera footage, weather data, and the other driver’s description. A pattern of repeated claims, recently expanded coverage, rapid reporting after a policy change, or the same repair facility across unrelated files can justify referral under the organization’s rules. Privacy and due-process requirements still apply, and a referral is not proof of fraud.

For a claimant with genuine pre-existing damage, the correct path is to disclose it, request a causation inspection, and ask the insurer to separate old and new repairs. Keep authentic photographs and invoices, and challenge a mistaken assessment through the policy’s appeal or appraisal process. The training value lies in consistent evidence handling and fair detection; a staged-loss script, fabricated paperwork, or coaching for an interview would cross the line into facilitating fraud.

The file may also show a request that a preferred shop use a vague description or that inspection be delayed. An investigator verifies the shop independently, preserves originals and metadata, and compares the document dates with payment and service records. A claimant’s statement is recorded accurately; staff should never supply a preferred story.

The physical comparison examines reported direction, height, and force alongside deformation, paint transfer, broken fasteners, exposed material, debris, corrosion, dirt in a crease, previous filler, and repair seams. Reviewers compare purchase photographs, prior inspections, maintenance records, telematics, nearby cameras, police information, weather, witness accounts, and the other driver’s statement. One inconsistency is not proof, so the claimant receives a fair chance to explain.

A fraud team may also look for repeated claims, recent coverage changes, shared repair facilities, recurring witnesses, and inconsistent dates, subject to privacy and due-process rules. For genuine old damage, the proper path is to disclose it, describe what changed after the accident, request a causation inspection, and obtain separate old and new scopes. A mistaken assessment can be challenged through an independent estimate, appraisal, or appeal.

I will not provide a staged-collision script, a fabricated receipt, a false interview narrative, or advice for evading an adjuster. The case file is useful only for prevention: it shows where physical evidence, authentic records, and a truthful account can separate a legitimate repair dispute from intentional deception.
